::: {.hero-bio}

I am a PhD candidate in Economics at Universitas Indonesia, working in
development economics and urban and regional economics. My dissertation,
*Shaking Land and Shaking Lives*, asks how large seismic shocks reshape social
order, household behaviour, and local economies in Indonesian villages. The
first chapter is supported by a research grant from the ReCIPE Programme (CEPR
and UK FCDO). I also work as a teaching assistant in the graduate econometrics
sequence at Universitas Indonesia, across the master's and doctoral programmes.

Alongside my academic work I have spent a decade in Indonesian public
procurement, in provincial government roles and as a nationally certified
facilitator, competency assessor, and advisor.

:::

## Selected research

:::: {.paper}

::: {.paper-title}

Motive Without Mobilization? Earthquakes and Communal Conflict in Indonesia

:::

::: {.paper-meta}

Dissertation chapter &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Working paper]{.paper-status}

:::

::: {.paper-abstract}

Damage-level shaking cuts reported communal conflict by 1.5 percentage points,
yet theft rises by 5.8 points on the same villages in the same waves. Disasters
appear to change the composition of local violence rather than its level.

:::

::: {.paper-links}

[Draft (PDF)](files/paper1-motive-without-mobilization.pdf) [Details](research.qmd)

:::

::::

:::: {.paper}

::: {.paper-title}

Faith after the Shock: Earthquakes, Religious Expenditure, and the Insurance
Value of Religion in Indonesia

:::

::: {.paper-meta}

[Work in progress]{.paper-status}

:::

::: {.paper-abstract}

Whether religion functions as informal insurance against uninsured risk is
usually tested on stated religiosity. This project instead uses household
expenditure in rupiah, combined with village-level earthquake exposure, to
separate the income effect from the club-good and coping channels.

:::

::: {.paper-links}

[Details](research.qmd)

:::
